Feluda.description: A private investigator renowned for his sharp observation and deductive skills, also known as Prodosh C. Mitter.

Tapesh.description: Feluda's young cousin who often accompanies him on investigations and narrates the stories.

Kailash Chowdhury.description: A lawyer and former shikari from a zamindar family; his identical twin brother Kedar impersonates him to steal a valuable stone.

Abanish.description: Kailash Chowdhury's nephew, a passionate philatelist (stamp collector) who lives with him and becomes involved in the mystery.

Ganapati Chatterjee.description: Feluda's friend who lives near Kailash Chowdhury's house and helps Feluda by providing access to his rooftop for observation.

Emperor Aurangzeb.description: A Mughal emperor of India, referenced in relation to a missing diamond ring case solved by Feluda.

Sherlock Holmes.description: The famous fictional British detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle, often cited as Feluda's inspiration.

Shyampukur.description: A locality in Calcutta (now Kolkata), where Kailash Chowdhury's house is located.

Rajshahi.description: A region in present-day Bangladesh, formerly part of Bengal, where the Chowdhury family owned land.

Calcutta.description: The former name of Kolkata, a major city in India and the primary setting for the story.

Partition.description: Refers to the 1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan, which led to mass migrations.

Jaldapara Reserve Forest.description: A wildlife sanctuary in West Bengal, India, known for its elephant population.

Amrita Bazar Patrika.description: A historic English-language newspaper published in India, where Kailash Chowdhury saw Feluda's advertisement.

Victoria Memorial.description: A large marble building and museum in Kolkata, serving as a key location in the story.

Park Street Post Office.description: A well-known post office in Kolkata, referenced as the origin of the threatening letter.

Madhya Pradesh.description: A central Indian state, where Kailash Chowdhury claims to have found the valuable stone.

Switzerland.description: A European country, mentioned as the place where Kedar went to work in watchmaking.

Marwaris.description: An Indian ethnic group from Rajasthan, referenced as a family visiting Victoria Memorial.

Lower Circular Road.description: A major road in Kolkata, near the Victoria Memorial.

Chowringhee.description: A prominent area in central Kolkata, known for its commercial and cultural significance.

Calcutta Club.description: A prestigious social club in Kolkata, mentioned as a landmark.

Jabalpore.description: Jabalpur (also spelled Jabalpore) is a city in Madhya Pradesh, India, where Kailash Chowdhury bought the stone.

Indian Airlines.description: A former major domestic airline in India, referenced regarding Kedar's attempted escape to Bombay.

Bombay.description: The former name of Mumbai, a major Indian city.

supari.description: Areca nut, often chewed in India as a mild stimulant, sometimes with betel leaf.

zamindars.description: Landowners, often hereditary, who collected taxes and held significant power in colonial and pre-colonial India.

shikar.description: The act of hunting, especially big game, in India.

shikari.description: A hunter, particularly one who hunts large or dangerous animals.

Namaskar.description: A respectful Indian greeting, similar to 'hello' or 'greetings'.

rasgulla.description: A popular Bengali sweet made from ball-shaped dumplings of chhena (cottage cheese) cooked in sugar syrup.

pyjama-kurta.description: Traditional Indian attire consisting of loose trousers (pyjama) and a long tunic (kurta).

Babu.description: A term of respect or endearment in Bengali and Hindi, often used for educated or elderly men.

philately.description: The collection and study of postage stamps.

ayahs.description: Female domestic helpers or nannies, especially those who care for children.

paisa.description: A unit of currency in India, equal to one hundredth of a rupee.

jalebi.description: A sweet Indian dessert made by deep-frying batter in circular shapes and soaking them in sugar syrup.
